items.prose: Take $f(z) = \operatorname{Im} z$. Its quotient is $\frac{\operatorname{Im} h}{h}$.
items.question: What are the quotients for real $h$ and for imaginary $h = ik$?

options.text: 0 and $-i$, so $\operatorname{Im} z$ has no complex derivative
0 and 1, so it has no derivative
0 both times, so the derivative is 0
options.why: For $h = ik$, $\operatorname{Im} h = k$, so the quotient is $k/(ik) \ne 0$.

options.text: 1 both times, so the derivative is 1
options.why: For real $h$, $\operatorname{Im} h = 0$, so the quotient is 0.

feedback.correct: Real $h$: $0/h = 0$. Imaginary $h = ik$: $k/(ik) = -i$. Two limits, no derivative.

items.question: What is $\operatorname{Log}(-1 - i)$?

items.question: By what factor does $1/z$ stretch small shapes near $z = 2$?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Differentiate $z^{-1}$ and take the modulus.

byKey.sign: A stretch is a modulus, so it is positive. The minus sign is a half turn.

explain.text: $f'(z) = -z^{-2}$, so $f'(2) = -\frac14$: shapes shrink to a quarter and turn by 180 degrees.

items.question: For which pricer does it give the right derivative?

options.text: One that uses `max(x - K, 0)` on the real part
options.why: `.real` throws away the imaginary part, so the step returns 0.
`abs` is not analytic: it ignores the direction of the step.
The trick needs $f$ complex differentiable along the path of the step.

feedback.correct: Only analytic pieces carry $ihf'(x)$ through to the imaginary part.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which operations are complex differentiable?

explain.text: $f(x + ih) \approx f(x) + ihf'(x)$ only when $f$ is complex differentiable. Sums, products, quotients and `cmath.exp` are; `abs`, `max` and `.real` are not.

items.prose: Complex powers: $2^i = e^{i\ln 2}$, using the principal logarithm.
items.question: What is the real part of $2^i$?

byKey.mod: $|2^i| = 1$: an imaginary power only turns. The real part is $\cos(\ln 2)$.

explain.text: $2^i = e^{i\ln 2}$ is on the unit circle at angle $\ln 2 \approx 0.6931$ radians. Its real part is $\cos(0.6931) \approx 0.7692$.
